heading: 1731 — Census Commentary, the De la Fontaine Report
text: 1731 — Census Commentary, the De la Fontaine Report
html: 1731 — Census Commentary, the De la Fontaine Report

anchors.name: ft_ch_1731 The De la Fontaine Report

text: 30th January, 1732 Algemeen Rijksarchief Collectie Rademacher Inv. Nr. 507
Compiled and prepared for computer output by Leonard Guelke, Robert Shell and Anthony Whyte
html:
Compiled and prepared for computer output by
Leonard Guelke, Robert Shell and Anthony Whyte

text: By 1732 a new Cape Town patrician society had emerged, composed of the elite officialdom intermarried with the wealthiest burghers of the town.  These become known as the Mamluks of Cape Town.  Jan de la Fontaine  ushered in this new era in 1729, the first Governor to be married to a local Cape Town woman, Maria Elisabeth de Mann. In 1711, at the age of twenty she married de la Fontaine, the young energetic Company employee, who had arrived at the Cape in March of 1710 on the Horstendal .
html: By 1732 a new Cape Town patrician society had emerged, composed of the elite officialdom intermarried with the wealthiest burghers of the town. These become known as the Mamluks of Cape Town. Jan de la Fontaine ushered in this new era in 1729, the first Governor to be married to a local Cape Town woman, Maria Elisabeth de Mann. In 1711, at the age of twenty she married de la Fontaine, the young energetic Company employee, who had arrived at the Cape in March of 1710 on the Horstendal .

text: In addition to its regular cargo, the Horstendal  carried slaves from the Eastern possessions.  Transporten, T 1710, no 256 (22 March, 1710) "Joost Maree to Anthonij Abrahams" Carel 14 years old; No 259 from the Skipper, Jacobus Hellama to Helena Bezuidenhout, weduwee van Jan Wessels.  * De In Fontaine's first recorded act in the Cape was to import a slave-Leander of Batavia-from Carel Lavin, the skipper of the De Waarde in the first month of his stay at the Cape.  Transporten, T1710 No 283 (29 March 1710).  * To understand the formation of the Mamluks one has to understand the slave trade.

text: According to his biographer, the hard-working De La Fontaine was soon promoted in 1711 to master of the Warehouses and also became a member of the Orphan Chamber. It was perhaps in his duties on that board he became acquainted with his future wife, who must have been a ward of that body since her wealthy father had died when she was four. In 1727 he requested to be relieved of his company service. The Cape Council of Policy however forwarded him as their candidate for Governor. The Directors in Holland  refused his request for resignation, provided him with a promotion and a substantial increase in salary.

text: Evidently the Directors in Holland trusted De La.Fontaine. In his first years as governor he wrote an extraordinary, secret commentary an each of the burghers and free blacks of the Cape Colony, including a separate list of all those who had repatriated before 1732. Gerrit Schutte in Holland is the only historian apart from ourselves to have worked on the first of these. The repatriated list is therefore quite novel to all South African historians (see illustrations).

text: In the year following his report, he was made Councillor Extraordinary of India, although he stayed at the Cape, which was now governed from Holland, not Batavia. The wealthy urban burghers now had a protective, controlling voice on the Council of Policy, indeed the governor was now one of them and we can talk of the golden age of the Mamluks.

text: A new intermarried and harmonious patriciate emerged which dominated the slave trading and commercial interests of the port until well after 1778. Perhaps it is no coincidence that the system of registering slaves publicly no longer occurs after 1731. The information on his list is invaluable in terms of the rate of indebtedness and emigration from the colony and the occupational structure of town and country. The document is weakest on the free blacks. With a few exceptions, de La Fontaine only gives them a formulaic description.

text: The original source looks quite different. First, there are really two lists, one of burghers ("BURG") in our list, and two a list of all persons who repatriated ("REPA")-he is really harsh on these in his commentary-Second, his lists are alphabetized by first name, within the three districts of the Cape, ("CAPE") Stellenbosch ("STELL") and Drakensteijn ("DRAK") which was the custom in the small Cape community of the eighteenth century. We have combined these two lists and alphabetized them by last name, which enhances the accessibility for twentieth century researchers. To each householder we added an Identity number ("IDNO") which represents the exact order of the householder's appearance on the original document. A future addition might include the list of names arranged in their original order so that neighborhoods might be reconstructed. In all other respects the words are the same as on the original documents. Editorial brackets indicate our updating of spelling.

text: Introduction to the court records in Changing Hands
html: Introduction to the court records in Changing Hands

text: The Court records (both civil and criminal) comprise several hundred meters of shelf space in the Hague and at the Cape. They are fine sources for historians. Hans Heese, Robert Ross, Nigel Worden and Gerald Groenewald have all used them to brilliant effect (the latter most recently in the classic 2006 Van Riebeeck Society volume).

text: One does wonder if the Cape crime records are complete. While in Holland the compiler came across a major master and slave case involving Christiaan Gottlieb Opperman, 1696-1737, the stamvader, who tortured and killed his slave Dam in 1730. The grisly case was more than a hundred folios long. I have included my notes here under the year 1731. One notes that Opperman’s case does not figure in the criminal sentences of the Cape 1652 to 1827 (included here, courtesy of the National Archives and Clive Kirkwood), nor in Hans Heese’s exact compilation in Reg en Onreg. This raises the question whether we need a full comparison of the crime records, both metropolitan and local.

text: Patriarchs and paternalists at the Cape had one thing in common: both wanted obedience from their slaves. The patriarch, however, was willing to kill his slave to obtain it even though this meant losing property. The paternalist, on the other hand, expected love and obedience from his slave.  In this volume, Opperman represents the patriarch; Samuel Hudson (q.v.) the paternalist.

In this volume, Opperman represents the patriarch; Samuel Hudson (q.v.) the paternalist.

text: When Georg Willhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831) wrote his account of the master and slave relationship, he might well have had in mind the Cape slave owner Christiaan Gottlieb Opperman and his slave, Dam. Most of the elements of Hegel’s thinking on the master/slave relationship are imbedded in Dam’s gruesome tale. Hegel argued that because the slave has already forfeited his life, he has nothing to lose and is, in a sense, free. This is based on the mort vivant [the living dead] view of slavery in which the captor spares the life of the vanquished and makes him or her a slave. In this transaction the captor obtains honor while the captured person enters slavery. Hegel’s slave’s rejection of the slave status finds an echo in Dam’s for running away twice before his final punishment: before his murder, Dam simply does not acknowledge his slave status. Opperman therefore claims the captor’s privilege of taking the life of the slave. The master, in Hegel’s view, however, loses both his property and his  honor when he kills his slave, therefore, he is not in control of his slave in the sense that we ordinarily view and think about the master/slave relationship. This irony must eventually transform and end the state of slavery.

text: Christiaan Gottlieb Opperman was born in the German port of Krossen in 1696. We know little of his early life, except that he was presumably raised a Reformed Christian. He also claimed to have enjoyed something of an education. In his interrogation and in informal conversations with Cape burghers he claimed that his father had spent a good deal of money on his education. Some of that education must have been in law. He evidently knew his bible quite well, at least the Old Testament. He also claimed to know more about the “African politics” than anyone at the Cape. He also wrote fluently in German, rather than Dutch. By the standards of the Cape, Opperman was a well-educated man.

text: We do not know why Opperman left his homeland. He came to the Cape in 1725 at the rank of a Dutch East India Company soldier. He was promoted to “assistant” in 1727 and was married on the 6th February, 1729 to Maria Koster, the 26 year-old widow of the Cape silversmith and wealthy farmer, Conrad Feyt. Opperman was, according to all the genealogists, a stamvader, equivalent to one of America's “first families.” He appears in all the genealogies. No scholar has ever mentioned that Opperman was notorious at the Cape. He was the first settler to kill one of his slaves and get away with the homicide.  His dismissal of all the regular patrician officers of justice at the Cape, from the Fiscal to the Caffers; his insistence on using “his own law;” his legal defense i.e. his slaves were his property and his armed solo defense of his werf strike one as the quintessential characteristics of the emerging Cape patriarch whose credo was in sharp contrast to that of the patrician officers of the DEIC. He treated his children and his slaves without distinction. Both his slaves, natural children and his wife betrayed him. Opperman believed his home was cursed and wanted to return to the “Fatherland.” He did, but returned.

text: This set of documents, selected from over a hundred folios of dramatic court testimony and related evidence, tell their own story of the special domestic arena in early South Africa, a patriarchal household. As Oscar Wilde observed there is nothing so dramatic as failure: in Opperman's domestic failure which resulted in these documents the otherwise obscure and intricate workings of the patriarchal household are dramatically exposed. Opperman died in 1737 at the age of 41, leaving two children and a divorced wife.

text: After completing the investigation we found a wound which went through to the bone across the left hand with a length of two “great” inches, and one above the third segment of the right middle finger right through to the bone so that the finger itself was hanging only by the muscles and tendons. [We also found] one [wound] in the right [dice?] approximately the size of two inches broad and with a depth of one inch and from the top to the bottom three inches which was a three-cornered wound. This wound was caused by an extremely sharp instrument. None of these wounds were potential fatal, except perhaps the latter, which could have resulted in sudden death because much blood could have been lost. But this did not happen as the wound had sealed itself with scabs. We found various other wounds on the right side and the left side which were also caused by a sharp instrument. There was considerable contusion of the muscles two on the right buttock, one on the outer muscle of the left buttock and a burn on the upper lip all of which were occasioned by burning. None of these latter wounds were fatal.

This wound was caused by an extremely sharp instrument. None of these wounds were potential fatal, except perhaps the latter, which could have resulted in sudden death because much blood could have been lost. But this did not happen as the wound had sealed itself with scabs. We found various other wounds on the right side and the left side which were also caused by a sharp instrument. There was considerable contusion of the muscles two on the right buttock, one on the outer muscle of the left buttock and a burn on the upper lip all of which were occasioned by burning. None of these latter wounds were fatal.

text: Signed, J.V. Schoor and B.D. Jean.
Testimony: Baajou van Batavia  contra Opperman5

A runaway slave boy of his master's named Dam was brought to his master's farm “The Brewery.” His master, Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman, had his slave Dam beaten on the bare buttocks by two of his slaves, Alexander and David, for the length of time it takes to smoke a pipe, with canes where he had just previously been beaten by the caffers  so that the flesh on his buttocks was broken and much blood flowed. [Although] the burgher Peter Breda, Master Gobbelaar, a tailor living here named Christiaan, and a knecht of Mr. Swellengebel, named Matthijs, and even Opperman's own wife, spoke in the slave boy's favor, yet would Opperman refuse to listen.

text: He got off his horse and beat Dam (who had been forced to carry a wheel on his shoulder for the whole day) with his club for as long as he was able. One of the people from the barn, Jan, was present when Opperman began to beat the slave boy and as he was about to leave, Dam's owner asked “Dog, will you not stand up. I will beat you to death [doodslaan].” The slave boy Dam then did his utmost and tried to stand up but was unable to; then Opperman took a stick of burning wood which he held under Dam's nose and Dam began to murmur. At this Opperman said, “Aij! My boy so now you can speak, tell me what happened on the mountain?” Whereupon Dam answered “I was visiting there.” To which Opperman answered, “Then you can also visit here.”

text: Testimony: Alexander van Bengal  [Opperman's slave, age 34] 6

The slave boy Dam at nine o'clock in the evening cried out three times “Oh God.” He was approaching death when a slave of Opperman's, Baajou, who was in the kitchen, heard Opperman say, “Is the dog dead? Take him away and cover him with a bag.” The aforementioned Hofman, talking with the witness the day before, had told him that he must not tell the fiscal what he had seen. The witness replied that on the contrary what he had seen he would have to testify to.

text: The previous Sunday in the morning between ten and eleven o'clock a runaway slave Dam was brought by two slaves of Opperman's to his farm the Brewery. Dam was tied fast with a rope on Opperman's orders and hung from a tree, Opperman then placed a basket full of acorns under his feet and forced Dam to tread them with his feet till three in the afternoon. Opperman, himself, then untied him and threw him to the ground; whereupon the slaves Alexander and David on the orders of Opperman beat Dam with several canes on the bare buttocks where he had been beaten by the caffers and continued beating him for half an hour. In between the beatings Dam was rubbed over his whole body with salt and pepper. Much blood spurted from the slave boy's body. Master Gibbe¬laar, the burgher Pieter Breda and the tailor Christoffel and a knecht of the elderly, honorable Swel¬lengrebel called Matthijs, were all present.

text: After the slave boy Dam was so shamefully beaten, the accused baas7 Opperman took a heavy iron chain attached to a wheel which was attached in turn to a smaller chain which he attached to the leg of the slave. The slave boy was forced to carry the wheel on his shoulders and simultaneously also to dig with a pick and a shovel working on the reeds in the garden. When the slave Dam disappeared among those tall reeds he (the witness) saw Opperman send his slaves to the garden to look for Dam. Soon after this Opperman went to the farm with the aforementioned company and the burgher, Ten Hoolten, who had arrived in the meanwhile. The slave boy Dam was found and dragged out of the reeds by the witness himself. Dam, tied with a heavy chain to a wheel so that with the weight of the wheel and the continuation of the beating, could no longer stand up. Opperman then miserably kicked him with both feet, so excessively that the others, among them the recently arrived Ten Holden who told Opper¬man to leave off. Whereupon Opperman said, “What! Leave off? Such scum must be beaten.” By this time dusk had fallen. Opperman brought Dam back and put him into the smoke house [ stookgat] till the next day.

text: On the next day, i.e. on the 26th of February [sic, January?], the slave owner Opperman had to ride to the Cape [to town] but before leaving had Dam tied with the same wheel on his shoulders and ordered that he should remain on the farm [werf]. Opper¬man returned at three in the afternoon under the influence of drink. Dam was leaning in ex¬haustion against a beer vat with the wheel on the ground. Seeing this Opperman then began to beat him with a sjambok and continued until he [Opperman] could beat the slave no more, whereupon he went into the house to rest, and put a pair of slippers on his feet. He then returned and saw Dam lying on the ground again and he shouted at Dam to stand up, but Dam was in no condition to do this. He then began to beat Dam with a rough piece of timber [swarop] for such a long time that the wood broke. Dam fainted from the severity of these blows. Opperman then called to Valentijn to bring a rope and ordered him and another slave, Baajou, to tie the hands of the slave boy Dam together and hoist him up by the wrists onto a branch of a tree while Opperman threw three buckets of water, one after the other, at the slave's head. Seeing that the slave boy Dam, through all this torture, had lost consciousness, Opperman decided to call to the slave girl  Hansje to bring a piece of burning wood which he first placed between Dam's legs [onder de billen = lit. under the buttocks] and then under the unconscious Dam's nose. After this the witness with the slave  Baajou, released Dam and took him to the smoke house in which Opperman locked him. Before long, after the length of time it takes to smoke a pipe, when it grew dark Opperman opened the smoke house and stepped in and began again to beat the prone and almost dead slave boy Dam with pick and spade until he [Opperman] could no longer hold anything in his hands anymore. Opperman then pierced various holes in Dam's body and when his rage had cooled he had the un¬fortunate Dam dragged to the kitchen by slaves,  Alexander and  Macca, with the same chain on his leg. A soldier from the fort named  Hofman witnessed all this. The slave died at nine o`clock in the evening in the kitchen,  whereupon  Baajou went and told his baas Opperman who was sitting on a stone bench on a bridge that was near to the kitchen. Opperman said “Is the dog dead? Let him be dragged away and covered with a sack.”

text: That is the month of June, the previous year, according to the witness' best recollection, he, with the burghers, Gerrit van Kerke, Jacob de Vries and Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman rode together from the farm of the first mentioned to Tijgerberg, arriving that day on the farm of the widow of Samuel Walters. That he spent the previous day riding around Tijgerberg and returned in the evening to the widow Walters and there met the son of widow Walters called Peter van Neiuwkerken, to drink a friendly glass of wine. The aforesaid Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman after they had spoken on many things burst out and said that no one in Africa understood politics as he did, that he had studied, that it had cost his father enough. Whereupon widow Walters said, “Be ashamed, to say you alone understand politics. I have been here so long and ruled by our Lords and Masters. How could that be without politics?” At this the witness Van Helsdingen stood up from the bench where he was sitting with Peter van Nieuwkerken, and said: “Mr. Opperman, let us keep quiet about these matters and talk over a glass of wine.” The aforementioned Opperman stood up from his chair and answered the witness: “In that case I respect you no more than a slave, to come and correct me here.” Then the witness heard certainly ugly words. He couldn't remember whether Opperman gave him a push on the chest with his hand. Whereupon he said: “How dare you take me for a slave. I claim to be a man as much as you do and even though you have read so much and so broadly you yourself then do slaves' work. [Opperman then pushes him across the room, draws a bayonet and is locked up by the widows].

All present. The council is ordered by the Governor to hear verbally the following report of the evil reception which greeted the committee members on the farm, called “the Brewery” owned by the burgher, Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman:
html: All present. The council is ordered by the Governor to hear verbally the following report of the evil reception which greeted the committee members on the farm, called “the Brewery” owned by the burgher, Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman:

text: Monday 27th February 1731: Present: the Lord Adriaan van Kervel, and the officials of the Fiscal's office, the honorable Johannes Thobias Rhenius and Paulus Artois.
html: Monday 27th February 1731: Present: the Lord Adriaan van Kervel, and the officials of the Fiscal's office, the honorable Johannes Thobias Rhenius and Paulus Artois.

text: This afternoon about one 'o clock...rode out to the farm of the burgher Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman lying near the Newlands to inspect there the dead body of a slave boy of Opperman's, of which report was brought to him, arriving at the farm after a little over two hours ride. A little way from the coach, we met with the same Opperman in a tipsy state, who took off his hat to greet us. Whereupon the fiscal said, “Mr Opperman, you asked this morning for my permission to bury a young slave boy which I cannot give without first seeing the boy and so I have come here with instructions from the Council of Justice.” His worship then asked where the body was. Whereupon Opperman replied: ”The slave boy is in the kitchen. He hanged himself yesterday because of despondency, having previously been beaten for running away and forced to carry a heavy wheel on his shoulders, up and down the farm. He had first wounded himself all over his body.” And while the dead body was carried out of the kitchen and placed on a table outside the Fiscal said to Opperman: “You did well to ask me if the slave could be buried, but you did not inform me that he died this way.” Opperman answered thus: “It is true, Sir, that I should have done so but it didn't occur to me.” Then followed the inspection of the dead body by the surgeon general of the Government, Jan van Schoor, during which Opperman said that the slave had hanged himself, and Opperman asked another of his slaves who was standing near us where the slave had hanged himself, and the latter replied: “Sir, the slave did not hang himself.” Opperman forcefully interjected that the slave had died thus and that he himself had called for a piece of burning wood from the kitchen to place under the slave's nose to see whether he still lived. Therefore our close investigation of the case was absurd and served no purpose. The fiscal told Opperman most courteously that he should have had the dead body taken to Cape Town. Opperman became so arrogant at this questioning as to ask who would bear the cost of that and to say further, “I have no wagon or oxen.” Whereupon the Fiscal, quietly and earnestly urged him that the means should have been found. All this time Opperman could not remain peaceable, continued in his disrespectful bearing, without once removing his hat, so that the first signatory below (undersigned) [Rhenius], to make an end of the case, said to the fiscal: “Sir, be so good as to have the executioner and the caffers come.” At these words the aforesaid Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman, whose conscience surely gnawed at him, became so angry, that he failed to consider that the caffers were summoned, not for him, but to give any slaves on the place a chance to clarify the death of the slave boy Dam, and forthwith turning his back on us and walked towards the house saying insolently: “Then I will use my own law,” though he seemed also to our amazement and consternation to be deathly pale. We saw Opperman immediately then, with his head covered, leaning against the small narrow window of a room, facing onto the farm, one hand upon the window sill, the other hand downwards so that we could not see what he was holding in it, although we believed he concealed a pistol or other firearm, his being so wild and incensed. The Honorable Fiscal, having with all of us gathered in front of that little window, asked Opperman why he treated the law in such a way, and locked himself in that little room, which was very suitable to Opperman's wicked intention, being very small and having but one window before which one could hardly stand or lean and locked from within. Opperman then uttered many threatening words to the effect that he understood from what the first undersigned said that he would be taken into custody and had taken steps to prevent it, he also said he had a clean conscience and nothing to burden him, that it was planned to deal with him “ab executione” that if the Fiscal had any evidence against him his worship could summon him before the Council to which he would answer. After this there poured from his mouth many no less disrespectful, tumultuous and threatening words, during which time he refused to listen to anything the Fiscal said, who assured him we had not come to apprehend him or injure him in the slightest but only to inspect the dead body of the slave and then to take steps to give the slaves there a chance to witness to the truth. The aforesaid Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman then leant back (yielded) a little and we saw on both sides of the little window a rifle, also an harquebus on its trestle,11 one more short rifle and further into the room on a rack, more rifles. The first undersigned saw the bold and really threatening demeanor which Opperman presented to us, and could not on this account refrain from rebuking Opperman with sharp words and threatening treatment, such would bring a furious man to his senses (himself), at which he became so angry that he pulled his head back into his hat, went to lean in his former posture against the window, and we heard among other things: “I would rather leave this world, Mr. Rhenuis. Could you not help me, I beg you help me. You would please me. I would fain be as far beneath the ground as I am now above it.” So Opperman made known to us all that he had resolved on a great wrongdoing and that he only waited for the opportunity and so we were in great uneasiness that he would injure one of us, so that at last after many words had passed to and fro, the undersigned, seeing that Opperman was beyond reason and apprehensive of calamity, the more so when a slave boy came to warn us that Opperman's little daughter had said that her father had loaded his gun, left the window to stand at a corner of the house, where Opperman came to find us. Having from us the assurance that no harm would befall him, he was nevertheless without any diminution of the savagery and threat in his countenance, and bitterly complained that an injury had been done to him, saying also domestic affliction had befallen him, thereupon the Fiscal asked Opperman what or who stood in his way, and what people persecuted him, to which Opperman answered that he could not speak of these things in that place but that he would come to the first meeting of the Council of Policy and do so there and also ask for his return to the fatherland and after addressing these words to the Fiscal Opperman continued: “I hope Sir, that you will not oppose my request because I will take it upon my soul and conscience.” After this we rode away to return to the Cape and report to His Worship the Governor, Jan de la Fontaine.

The Honorable Fiscal, having with all of us gathered in front of that little window, asked Opperman why he treated the law in such a way, and locked himself in that little room, which was very suitable to Opperman's wicked intention, being very small and having but one window before which one could hardly stand or lean and locked from within. Opperman then uttered many threatening words to the effect that he understood from what the first undersigned said that he would be taken into custody and had taken steps to prevent it, he also said he had a clean conscience and nothing to burden him, that it was planned to deal with him “ab executione” that if the Fiscal had any evidence against him his worship could summon him before the Council to which he would answer. After this there poured from his mouth many no less disrespectful, tumultuous and threatening words, during which time he refused to listen to anything the Fiscal said, who assured him we had not come to apprehend him or injure him in the slightest but only to inspect the dead body of the slave and then to take steps to give the slaves there a chance to witness to the truth. The aforesaid Gottlieb Christiaan Opperman then leant back (yielded) a little and we saw on both sides of the little window a rifle, also an harquebus on its trestle,11 one more short rifle and further into the room on a rack, more rifles. The first undersigned saw the bold and really threatening demeanor which Opperman presented to us, and could not on this account refrain from rebuking Opperman with sharp words and threatening treatment, such would bring a furious man to his senses (himself), at which he became so angry that he pulled his head back into his hat, went to lean in his former posture against the window, and we heard among other things: “I would rather leave this world, Mr. Rhenuis. Could you not help me, I beg you help me. You would please me. I would fain be as far beneath the ground as I am now above it.” So Opperman made known to us all that he had resolved on a great wrongdoing and that he only waited for the opportunity and so we were in great uneasiness that he would injure one of us, so that at last after many words had passed to and fro, the undersigned, seeing that Opperman was beyond reason and apprehensive of calamity, the more so when a slave boy came to warn us that Opperman's little daughter had said that her father had loaded his gun, left the window to stand at a corner of the house, where Opperman came to find us. Having from us the assurance that no harm would befall him, he was nevertheless without any diminution of the savagery and threat in his countenance, and bitterly complained that an injury had been done to him, saying also domestic affliction had befallen him, thereupon the Fiscal asked Opperman what or who stood in his way, and what people persecuted him, to which Opperman answered that he could not speak of these things in that place but that he would come to the first meeting of the Council of Policy and do so there and also ask for his return to the fatherland and after addressing these words to the Fiscal Opperman continued: “I hope Sir, that you will not oppose my request because I will take it upon my soul and conscience.” After this we rode away to return to the Cape and report to His Worship the Governor, Jan de la Fontaine.

text: In the event of the evil behavior against me and the subsequent hanging of this runaway of mine I was yesterday so overcome by mishap that as the honorable Captain, although obliged, adopted such a furious tone with me, by all accounts, yes even with caffers and executioners to oppose me, against such prostitution I resolved to resist, knowing well moreover, that it would not befit your worship that I was prostituted on my own land, regarding these matters the captain is far from being empowered to act and acts against me as a traitor. So I must, am forced, to request from your honor, to prevent further calamity, that you graciously agree to a “salvum conductum”: that I may thereby also enjoy the right to the advantage of your written word I have done nothing that so towards me one should seek to act “ab executione” (a course against all justice) but men can on such occasions [...] So I take refuge with your worship, in the right and laws of this land, in my affliction, in your continued observance of niceties, that my freedom will not be curtailed, to allow me to answer the charges against me, without the custody of so many soldiers, I console myself that in that case I will received a favorable hearing.

text: [Resolutions continue...] And while on the one hand nothing is easier than to deal with this man with force, to force obedience on him when he raises a armed hand against the law and seeks to oppose command, to overcome him, dead or alive. On the other hand, there is a fear that such an undertaking, in the circumstances of this case (he was armed and desperate) in view of his irascible nature, of which there are many examples, would very likely cost the lives of one or more men, to avert such a calamity, the Honorable Governor is respectfully advised to consider whether it would not be best first to attempt to bring the aforesaid Opperman here with a soft line, to reply to him in answer to his letter that His Honor dispatched the aforementioned company so that he could travel here under its protection and that he advises him yet again to proceed thus in order that other measures will not be rendered necessary, deserved by his disobedience and not pleasant as a result to him, with the assurance that otherwise nothing has been done to his disadvantage but on the contrary every thing has been done, in keeping with statutory law and the usual customs. Over these things we have deliberated. So it is unanimously resolved and decided to put this before the Honorable Governor.

text: In 1731 the free and slave population was concentrated in the south-western Cape. The slave population comprised a majority in the older rural areas, most noticeably in the Cape Peninsula (excluding Cape Town), the Tijgerberg-Swart-land and Stellenbosch. In Cape Town itself slaves outnumbered free people by a small margin. Only in the frontier areas did free Europeans comprise a majority of the opgaaf population. However, in these areas the Khoekhoe (who were not enumerated in the opgaaf) would have been by far the most numerous element in the population.

text: The slave population was characterized by uneven sex ratios. Adult males comprised from 75 to over 90 per cent of the total slave population in all areas, except in Cape Town where the figure was 55 per cent. The adult women slaves were never much more than 10 per cent of all slaves, with Cape Town again being the exception. In Cape Town slave women comprised just over 20 per cent of all slaves. text: Cape-born and -raised adults were everywhere in the vast majority, except for Cape Town. A few immigrants were found in rural areas; but not surprisingly most of these immigrants were males. Few female immigrants had made their way to the frontier regions. In 1731 the rural free population of the Cape was already a population rooted in the land, and population growth occurred by natural increase as well as immigration. This population had no difficulty in absorbing male immigrants who settled in the country. Cape Town as an urban centre in close touch with the outside world and having a large immigrant population of both males and females, was sharply distinguished from the rest of the colony.

text: The various ethnic groups comprising the Cape free population were not evenly distributed. A large number of Dutch, German, and French colonists had not yet welded together, although the vast majority of the Cape’s population (except for the people of Cape Town) was native born. The process of welding, however, was under way and the free ‘white’ population comprised a significant proportion of persons of mixed European and mixed European and African and Asian ancestry.

text: German males were less numerous than their Dutch counterparts and clustered in the agricultural areas near Cape Town. Many took slaves wives and these unions were solemnized in the Lutheran church when that religion was tolerated in 1779.

text: The free people of mixed racial ancestry were very much a colonial phenomenon. The males were well represented in Cape Town and Stellenbosch district, but were also found in other areas. The females were found scattered through the rural areas and in Cape Town. The females of mixed racial ancestry were more numerous than the males (48 as against 32). This fact is probably explained by the general shortage of women at the Cape, which would have made it easier for mixed-ancestry females to be assimilated into the ‘white’ population.

There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, Valentijn van de Caab, slave of the honourable Company, 32 years old at a guess, who, on the requisition of the honourable Independent Fiscal, Meester Daniel van den Henghel, confesses it to be true:

text: That he, the confessant, together with David, a slave of the honourable Company, had deserted about seven months ago, and during this time supported themselves by chopping and selling fire wood.
html: That he, the confessant, together with David, a slave of the honourable Company, had deserted about seven months ago, and during this time supported themselves by chopping and selling fire wood.

text: That recently there came to them a fellow slave of the honourable Company, Kindsa, with whom the confessant, came to the Cape one night, when the said Kindsa leaped into the corral of the widow of Servaas de Cok and stole from it two sheep, and brought these to the confessant, who was standing by the corral on this side of the ditch awaiting Kindsa. After which they each took a sheep onto their shoulders and, when they came close to the silk filatory with these [sheep], the aforementioned Kindsa was taken prisoner by the ratelwacht. When the confessant, who was walking behind [Kindsa], saw this, he threw down his sheep to the ground and fled; yet he was taken prisoner about a month ago now at night at the penfold by the burgerwacht.

text: That having been a deserter for about one month, the confessant was ordered by a former caffer, named Janbam, who was also a deserter, to go and steal a sheep from the corral of the honourable Company’s schuur. For which reason the confessant, now about two months ago, set out at 12 o’clock in the night with a fellow slave of the honourable Company, named Januarij, to the abovementioned corral into which the confessant leaped, took a sheep and threw it over the wall to the aforementioned slave Januarij. And just when the confessant wanted to take the second sheep, he heard a noise in the corral, on account of which he tried to get away from the corral but, as he was trying to leap over the wall, a European grabbed him by his legs; which European hit him with a small sword on his head when he tried to escape from him; and thus the confessant was delivered into the hands of justice the following day.

html: Compareerde voor ons ondergete. gecommitts. uijt den E. Achtb. Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements David van de Caab slaaf der E. Comp. oud omtrent 34 jaaren, dewelke ter requisitie van den Heer Independt. Fiscaal Mr. Daniel van den Henghel confesseerde hoe waar is:

text: Dat hij confesst. nevens den meede slaaf den E. Comp. Valentijn gent., omtrent een maand of seven heeft gedrost sijnde in dien tijd aan de kost gekomen met brand hout op ’t gebergte te kappen en hier aan de Caab te komen vercoopen en is hij confesst. des avonds om seven uuren aan de Caab komende door den burger Jan [onleesbaar] gevangen genomen.

text: Aldus geconfesseert aan Cabo de Goede Hoop den 23 Maij 1735.
html: Aldus geconfesseert aan Cabo de Goede Hoop den 23 Maij 1735.

text: Dit is ’t merk van David X.
Als gecommitts., [get.] H. Swellengrebel, R. Tulbagh.
Mij present, [get.] Js. de Grandpreez, secrets.

Compareerde voor ons ondergete. gecommitts. uijt den E. Achtb. Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements den slaaf David, dewelke deese sijne gegevene confessie van woord tot woord klaar en duijdelijk voorgeleesen sijnde verclaarde daarbij volkomen te persisteeren, niet begeerende oversulx datter iets meer bij gevoegt ofte van gedaan werden sal.

Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements den slaaf David, dewelke deese sijne gegevene confessie van woord tot woord klaar en duijdelijk voorgeleesen sijnde verclaarde daarbij volkomen te persisteeren, niet begeerende oversulx datter iets meer bij gevoegt ofte van gedaan werden sal.

text: Aldus gerecolleert aan Cabo de Goede Hoop den 24 Maij 1735.
html: Aldus gerecolleert aan Cabo de Goede Hoop den 24 Maij 1735.

text: Dit is ’t merk van den slaaf David X
html: Dit is ’t merk van den slaaf David X

text: Als gecommitts., [get.] H. Swellengrebel, R. Tulbagh.
Mij present, [get.] Js. de Grandpreez, secrets.

There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, David van de Caab, slave of the honourable Company, about 34 years old, who, on the requisition of the honourable Independent Fiscal Meester Daniel van den Henghel, confesses it to be true:
html: There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, David van de Caab, slave of the honourable Company, about 34 years old, who, on the requisition of the honourable Independent Fiscal Meester Daniel van den Henghel, confesses it to be true:

text: That the confessant, together with a fellow slave of the honourable Company, named Valentijn, having been deserters for about seven months, during which time they provided for themselves by chopping wood on the mountain and selling it here at the Cape, was taken prisoner by the burgher Jan [illegible] at about 7 o’clock in the evening when the confessant had come to the Cape.
html: That the confessant, together with a fellow slave of the honourable Company, named Valentijn, having been deserters for about seven months, during which time they provided for themselves by chopping wood on the mountain and selling it here at the Cape, was taken prisoner by the burgher Jan [illegible] at about 7 o’clock in the evening when the confessant had come to the Cape.

text: Thus confessed at the Cape of Good Hope, the 23rd of May 1735.
html: Thus confessed at the Cape of Good Hope, the 23rd of May 1735.

text: This X is the mark of David.
html: This X is the mark of David.

text: As delegates, [signed] H. Swellengrebel, R. Tulbagh.
In my presence, [signed] Js. de Grandpreez, secretary.
html: In my presence, [signed] Js. de Grandpreez, secretary.

text: There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, the slave David, who, after this, his given confession, was read out word by word, clearly and plainly, declares to fully persist by it, therefore not desiring that anything more should be added to or taken from it.
html: There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, the slave David, who, after this, his given confession, was read out word by word, clearly and plainly, declares to fully persist by it, therefore not desiring that anything more should be added to or taken from it.

text: Thus verified at the Cape of Good Hope, the 24th of May 1735.
html: Thus verified at the Cape of Good Hope, the 24th of May 1735.

text: This X is the mark of the slave David.
html: This X is the mark of the slave David.

text: As delegates, [signed] H. Swellengrebel, R. Tulbagh.
